q: Which country's flag has a red maple leaf in the middle?
x: The Maple Leaf flag was adopted in 1965, replacing the Canadian Red Ensign.

q: Which country's flag is a red circle on a plain white background?
x: Japan's flag is called the Hinomaru, 'circle of the sun'. Bangladesh also has a red disc, but on green.

q: Which country's national flag is nicknamed the Union Jack?
x: The Union Flag combines the crosses of St George (England), St Andrew (Scotland) and St Patrick (Ireland).

q: How many stars are on the flag of the United States?
x: One star for each state; the 13 stripes stand for the original 13 colonies. The 50-star version dates from 1960.

q: Which three colours make up the flag of Italy?
x: Italians call it il Tricolore: three vertical bands, green at the hoist. Green, white and orange is Ireland.

q: Which country's flag has a blue globe and a band of stars inside a yellow diamond on green?
x: The banner across the globe reads 'Ordem e Progresso' (Order and Progress). Its 27 stars stand for the states and the Federal District.

q: Which country has a square national flag with a white cross on red?
x: Switzerland and Vatican City are the only countries with square national flags. Denmark's white cross on red is rectangular and off-centre.

q: Which tree appears on the flag of Lebanon?
x: A green Lebanon cedar sits on a white band between two red bands.

q: What is shown in the middle of India's flag?
x: The navy-blue Ashoka Chakra, a wheel with 24 spokes, sits on the white band between saffron and green.

q: Which country's flag is a yellow cross on a blue background?
x: Finland has a blue cross on white, Norway a blue-and-white cross on red, Denmark a white cross on red.

q: Which country's flag shows an eagle eating a snake while perched on a cactus?
x: It recalls the Aztec legend of where to found their capital, Tenochtitlan, on the site of today's Mexico City.

q: Which country's flag is red with a white crescent and a white star?
x: Pakistan's crescent and star are white on green; Algeria's crescent is red; Malaysia's is yellow on blue.

q: Which country's flag has a white cross on red that is set towards the hoist side?
x: The Dannebrog is often said to be the oldest national flag still in use. Its off-centre 'Nordic cross' was copied by its neighbours.

q: Which country's flag has a black, gold and green diagonal cross?
x: Jamaica adopted the flag, with its gold saltire, at independence in 1962.

q: Which country's national flag is not a rectangle or a square, but two stacked triangles?
x: Nepal's flag is made of two pennants, one above the other, with a white moon and sun.

q: Which country's flag shows a white dragon?
x: Bhutan's name for itself, Druk Yul, means 'Land of the Thunder Dragon', and the Druk appears on its flag.

q: Which country's flag includes an AK-47 rifle?
x: The rifle is crossed with a hoe on top of an open book. Angola's flag has a half cogwheel and a machete.

q: Which country's flag carries a red-and-white chequered shield?
x: The chequerboard (šahovnica) sits in the middle of a red, white and blue tricolour.

q: Which country's flag has 14 red and white stripes?
x: The 14 stripes stand for the 13 states and the federal government. The US flag has 13 stripes, Liberia's 11.

q: Which country's flag has a broken trident in the middle?
x: The trident of Neptune, with its shaft broken off, stands for the island's break from colonial rule at independence in 1966.

q: Which country's flag shows a purple-and-green Sisserou parrot?
x: The Sisserou is Dominica's national bird and is found nowhere else in the world.

q: Which is the largest ocean?
x: The Pacific covers about a third of Earth's surface, more than all the land put together.

q: On which continent is the Sahara Desert?
x: The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world, stretching across much of North Africa.

q: Which is the highest mountain above sea level?
x: A joint China-Nepal survey in 2020 put Everest's height at 8,849 m.

q: Which river flows through London?
x: The Thames is about 346 km long. The Severn is the UK's longest river.

q: Which is the smallest continent by land area?
x: Australia covers about 7.7 million km². Europe is the second smallest.

q: On which continent is the Amazon rainforest?
x: Most of it is in Brazil, with the rest in eight other countries and territories.

q: The Strait of Gibraltar links the Atlantic Ocean to which sea?
x: At its narrowest, the strait between Spain and Morocco is less than 15 km wide.

q: Which is the longest river in Europe?
x: The Volga runs for about 3,500 km through Russia and empties into the Caspian Sea.

q: Which is the deepest lake in the world?
x: Baikal in Siberia is over 1,600 m deep and holds roughly a fifth of the world's unfrozen surface fresh water.

q: Which mountain range in Russia is usually taken as part of the boundary between Europe and Asia?
x: The Urals run roughly north to south for about 2,500 km, from the Arctic towards Kazakhstan.

q: Which two countries share the longest international border in the world?
x: Including Alaska's border with Canada, it runs for about 8,900 km. Russia and Kazakhstan share the second longest.

q: Not counting Australia, which is the largest island in the world?
x: Greenland covers about 2.2 million km². It is an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark.

q: Which river carries the most water into the sea?
x: The Amazon delivers roughly a fifth of all the river water that flows into the world's oceans.

q: Which country lies entirely inside South Africa?
x: Only three countries are completely surrounded by another one: Lesotho, and San Marino and Vatican City inside Italy.

q: Victoria Falls is on which river?
x: The falls are on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe. The local name, Mosi-oa-Tunya, means 'the smoke that thunders'.

q: Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest mountain, is in which country?
x: Kilimanjaro is a dormant volcano close to the Kenyan border, 5,895 m high.

q: Which is the longest mountain range on land?
x: The Andes run about 7,000 km down the western side of South America, through seven countries.

q: The shore of which body of water is the lowest point on land?
x: The Dead Sea shore is more than 400 m below sea level, and the water level is still falling.

q: The Atacama, one of the driest places on Earth, is mostly in which country?
x: Some weather stations in the Atacama have never recorded rain.

q: Which is the only sea with no land coastline?
x: The Sargasso Sea in the North Atlantic is bounded by ocean currents rather than land, and is named after its floating sargassum seaweed.

q: Counting its overseas territories, which country spans the most time zones?
x: Thanks to territories from French Polynesia to Réunion, France spans 12 time zones; Russia, on its own landmass, has 11.

q: Which country has the longest coastline in the world?
x: Canada's mainland and its thousands of Arctic islands give it a coastline of over 200,000 km.

q: Which country is often said to hold more than half of the world's lakes?
x: Canada has hundreds of thousands of lakes, many of them scooped out by glaciers during the last ice age.

q: Counting cold deserts, which is the largest desert on Earth?
x: A desert is defined by how little rain or snow falls, not by heat, and Antarctica gets very little of either.

q: Which is the largest country in the world by area?
x: Russia covers about 17.1 million km², roughly 11% of the world's land.

q: According to UN estimates, which country has had the most people since 2023?
x: The UN estimates India passed China during 2023. As of 2024 both have about 1.4 billion people.

q: Which is the smallest country in the world by area?
x: Vatican City covers less than half a square kilometre, entirely inside Rome.

q: Which is the largest country in South America by area?
x: Brazil covers nearly half of South America and borders every country on the continent except Chile and Ecuador.

q: Which continent has the most people?
x: About 60% of the world's people live in Asia.

q: Roughly how much of Earth's surface is covered by water?
x: Almost all of it is ocean; fresh water is only a small share of the total.

q: Which country has the most people in Africa?
x: As of 2024 Nigeria has over 220 million people; Ethiopia is second.

q: Which is the largest country in Africa by area?
x: Sudan was the largest until South Sudan became independent in 2011; since then it has been Algeria.

q: Which is the second-largest country in the world by area?
x: Canada covers about 10 million km², a little more than the United States or China.

q: Which country in the European Union has the most people?
x: As of 2024 Germany has about 84 million people, France about 68 million.

q: In which year did the world's population reach 8 billion, according to the UN?
x: The UN marked 15 November 2022 as the 'Day of Eight Billion'. The 7 billion mark was in 2011.

q: Which is the largest US state by area?
x: Alaska is more than twice the size of Texas, the second largest.

q: Which US state has the most people?
x: As of 2024 California has about 39 million people, Texas about 31 million.

q: Which country, made up entirely of islands, has the most people?
x: As of 2024 Indonesia has about 280 million people, spread over more than 17,000 islands.

q: Which is the largest country in the European Union by area?
x: Even without its overseas regions, France (about 550,000 km²) is bigger than second-placed Spain (about 506,000 km²).

q: According to UN estimates, which country has the third-largest population (as of 2024)?
x: About 340 million people, behind India and China. Indonesia is fourth.

q: Which is the largest lake in the world by surface area?
x: The salty Caspian covers about 370,000 km². Lake Superior is the largest freshwater lake by area.

q: Which is the largest landlocked country?
x: Kazakhstan covers about 2.7 million km², making it the ninth-largest country of all.

q: Which country is the most densely populated?
x: Monaco squeezes about 38,000 residents into around 2 km². Singapore leads among countries over 1 million people.

q: About how many people live in Greenland (as of 2024)?
x: The world's largest island has around 57,000 inhabitants, about a third of them in the capital, Nuuk.

q: Which is the largest country lying entirely in the Southern Hemisphere?
x: Brazil is bigger, but the equator crosses its north, so part of it is in the Northern Hemisphere.

q: In which city is the Colosseum?
x: The amphitheatre was finished in AD 80 and could hold tens of thousands of spectators.

q: In which country is Machu Picchu?
x: The Inca citadel was built in the 15th century high in the Andes, above the Urubamba valley.

q: Which city is overlooked by the Christ the Redeemer statue?
x: The statue was completed in 1931 on top of Corcovado mountain.

q: The Statue of Liberty was a gift to the United States from which country?
x: It was dedicated in New York Harbor in 1886. Gustave Eiffel's company engineered its inner frame.

q: In which city is the Sagrada Família?
x: Antoni Gaudí took charge of the basilica in 1883 and worked on it until his death in 1926.

q: In which city is the Brandenburg Gate?
x: The gate was completed in 1791. It stood just inside East Berlin while the Wall divided the city.

q: Which city is the Golden Gate Bridge in?
x: When it opened in 1937 it was the longest suspension bridge span in the world. Its colour is called International Orange.

q: The Eiffel Tower was built for which event?
w: The end of the First World War
x: It was the entrance arch to the 1889 Exposition Universelle and was meant to stand for only 20 years.

q: In which city is the Taj Mahal?
x: The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built it as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.

q: In which country is the ancient city of Petra?
x: The Nabataeans carved Petra's buildings straight into rose-coloured sandstone cliffs.

q: In which country is Angkor Wat?
x: Built in the 12th century, it is one of the largest religious monuments in the world, and it appears on Cambodia's flag.

q: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World is still standing?
x: It is also the oldest of the seven, built around 4,500 years ago, and was the tallest human-made structure for over 3,800 years.

q: Stonehenge is in which English county?
x: It stands on Salisbury Plain. Its first stage was built around 5,000 years ago.

q: As of 2026, which is the tallest building in the world?
x: The Dubai tower is 828 m tall and has held the record since it opened in 2010.

q: In which country is Neuschwanstein Castle?
x: King Ludwig II of Bavaria had it built from 1869. It is said to have inspired Disney's Sleeping Beauty castle.

q: Which city is home to the Hagia Sophia?
x: It was completed in 537 under the Byzantine emperor Justinian, and was the largest church in the world for nearly 1,000 years.

q: The giant stone Moai figures are on which island?
x: The island, called Rapa Nui by its people, is part of Chile, about 3,500 km off its coast.

q: Chichén Itzá in Mexico was a great city of which civilisation?
x: Its step pyramid, El Castillo, has stairways on all four sides.

q: In which Spanish city is the Alhambra palace?
x: The palace and fortress complex was built mainly in the 13th and 14th centuries by the Nasrid dynasty.

q: In which country is Borobudur, the world's largest Buddhist temple?
x: It was built on the island of Java in the 9th century.

q: A 2012 Chinese survey measured all the branches of the Great Wall of China. Roughly how long did it find it to be?
x: The survey counted 21,196 km of walls, trenches and natural barriers, built over many dynasties.

q: In which country are the ruins of Persepolis, the ancient Persian capital?
x: Darius the Great began building it around 518 BC.

q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
x: Mercury goes round the Sun once every 88 Earth days.

q: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
x: Its red colour comes from iron oxide, essentially rust, in its dust and rocks.

q: Which is the largest planet in the Solar System?
x: Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets put together.

q: How many sides does a hexagon have?
x: Honeybees build their combs from hexagonal cells, which use the least wax for the space they enclose.

q: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
x: It hangs in the Louvre in Paris, behind protective glass.

q: Who wrote the play Romeo and Juliet?
x: It was probably written in the mid-1590s and is set in Verona.

q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
x: Armstrong stepped onto the Moon during Apollo 11 in July 1969; Buzz Aldrin followed about 20 minutes later.

q: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
x: Au comes from the Latin word for gold, aurum. Ag is silver.

q: What is the hardest natural substance?
x: Diamond is pure carbon and scores 10, the top of the Mohs hardness scale.

q: Which gas makes up most of Earth's atmosphere?
x: Nitrogen is about 78% of the air and oxygen about 21%.

q: In which year did the Berlin Wall fall?
x: The border crossings opened on 9 November 1989; Germany was reunified less than a year later.

q: Which element has the atomic number 1?
x: Hydrogen is the lightest and most common element in the universe.

q: Who invented the World Wide Web?
x: He proposed it in 1989 while working at CERN, the physics laboratory near Geneva.

q: What is the smallest prime number?
x: 2 is also the only even prime. 1 doesn't count as a prime number.

q: Which language has the most native speakers?
x: Mandarin has over 900 million native speakers. English has the most speakers in total once second-language speakers are counted.

q: What is the longest bone in the human body?
x: The femur, or thigh bone, is also the strongest bone in the body.

q: Who wrote On the Origin of Species, published in 1859?
x: It set out his theory of evolution by natural selection, shaped partly by his voyage on HMS Beagle.

q: How many bones are in the adult human body?
x: Babies are born with more, around 300, and many of them fuse together as they grow.

q: Roughly how fast does light travel in a vacuum?
x: Exactly 299,792,458 metres per second. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth.

q: Which planet spins on its side, tilted at about 98 degrees?
x: One idea is that a huge collision long ago knocked it over.

q: As of 2025, which planet has the most known moons?
x: In 2025 astronomers announced 128 more small moons of Saturn, taking its count to 274, far ahead of Jupiter.

q: In which country were the first modern Olympic Games held, in 1896?
x: Athens hosted them, with athletes from 14 nations.

q: Which river flows through Paris?
x: The Seine rises in Burgundy and reaches the English Channel at Le Havre, passing through the heart of Paris on the way.

q: Which river flows through Cairo?
x: Almost all of Egypt's people live close to the Nile, because the rest of the country is mostly desert.

q: Mount Fuji is in which country?
x: Mount Fuji is an active volcano and Japan's highest mountain, at about 3,776 m. It last erupted in 1707.

q: Which ocean lies between Europe and North America?
x: The Atlantic is slowly getting wider, by a few centimetres a year, as the plates under it pull apart.

q: Which is the coldest continent?
x: The lowest air temperature ever measured, about -89 °C, was recorded at Vostok Station in Antarctica in 1983.

q: Mount Everest is part of which mountain range?
x: The name Himalaya comes from Sanskrit and means 'abode of snow'.

q: Which European country is famously shaped like a boot?
x: The 'toe' of the boot points towards Sicily, and the 'heel' is the region of Puglia.

q: Which imaginary line divides the Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres?
x: The Equator is about 40,000 km long, and places on it have roughly 12 hours of daylight all year round.

q: The Prime Meridian, 0° longitude, passes through which part of London?
x: It was agreed as the world's Prime Meridian in 1884, which is why time zones were once measured from Greenwich Mean Time (GMT).

q: Which desert covers much of Mongolia and northern China?
x: The Gobi is a cold desert: winter temperatures can drop below -30 °C. Many dinosaur fossils and eggs have been found there.

q: Which volcano buried the Roman town of Pompeii in AD 79?
x: Vesuvius, near Naples, is still active. Its last major eruption was in 1944.

q: Which country is made up mainly of the North Island and the South Island?
x: The two main islands are separated by Cook Strait. The South Island is the larger, but most people live on the North Island.

q: Niagara Falls lies on the border between Canada and which country?
x: The falls sit on the Niagara River, which drains Lake Erie into Lake Ontario.

q: Which country borders the United States to the south?
x: The US-Mexico border runs for about 3,100 km, from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf coast.

q: Which ocean surrounds the North Pole?
x: There is no land at the North Pole: it sits on sea ice floating on the Arctic Ocean, which is about 4 km deep there.

q: Which ocean surrounds Antarctica?
x: The Southern Ocean is defined by the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, the strongest ocean current on Earth.

q: What name is given to the horseshoe of volcanoes and earthquake zones around the Pacific Ocean?
x: Around three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes and most of its big earthquakes are found along the Ring of Fire.

q: What do we call an area of land almost surrounded by water but joined to the mainland?
x: The word comes from Latin for 'almost an island'. Spain and Portugal sit on the Iberian Peninsula.

q: What is molten rock called once it reaches the Earth's surface?
x: Underground the molten rock is called magma; it only becomes lava when it erupts out onto the surface.

q: Portugal shares a land border with only one country. Which?
x: The Spain-Portugal border is about 1,200 km long and one of the oldest borders in Europe.

q: The holiday island of Bali is part of which country?
x: Indonesia is made up of more than 17,000 islands, and Bali is one of the best known.

q: Which island country lies just off the south-east coast of India?
x: Sri Lanka is separated from India by the narrow Palk Strait, crossed by a chain of shoals called Adam's Bridge.

q: Which South American country is named after the Equator, which passes through it?
x: Ecuador is simply the Spanish word for 'equator'.

q: Which mountain range runs through western Canada and the western United States?
x: The Rockies stretch for about 4,800 km, from British Columbia down to New Mexico.

q: Which Italian city is built on more than 100 small islands in a lagoon?
x: Venice's islands are linked by around 400 bridges, and its canals take the place of streets.

q: Which US city stands at the mouth of the Hudson River?
x: Manhattan is an island between the Hudson River and the East River.

q: The city of Marrakesh is in which country?
x: Marrakesh lies at the foot of the Atlas Mountains and is famous for its huge market square, Jemaa el-Fnaa.

q: The port city of Alexandria, founded by Alexander the Great, is in which country?
x: Alexandria lies on the Mediterranean coast at the edge of the Nile Delta and is Egypt's second city.

q: What is the name for a long, narrow sea inlet between steep cliffs, carved by a glacier?
x: Norway's coast is famous for its fjords. Sognefjord is more than 200 km long.

q: What do we call the fan of land that forms where a river splits into many channels at its mouth?
x: It is named after the Greek letter delta (Δ), because the Nile Delta looked like a triangle to the ancient Greeks.

q: What is the word for a group or chain of islands?
x: Indonesia, the Philippines and Japan are all archipelagos.

q: Using the usual model taught in English-speaking schools, how many continents are there?
x: The seven are Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia (Oceania), Europe, North America and South America. Some countries teach six or five.

q: When it is summer in the UK, which season is it in Australia?
x: The seasons are reversed in the Southern Hemisphere, so many Australians have Christmas on the beach.

q: Loch Ness is in which part of the United Kingdom?
x: Loch Ness is so deep that it holds more fresh water than all the lakes in England and Wales put together.

q: Which sea lies between Great Britain and Scandinavia?
x: The North Sea is fairly shallow, averaging about 95 m deep, and much of its floor was dry land during the last Ice Age.

q: In which ocean are the Maldives?
x: The Maldives are made of coral atolls, and most of the land is only about a metre above sea level.

q: Jamaica and Cuba are islands in which sea?
x: The Caribbean Sea takes its name from the Carib people who lived in the region.

q: What is the name for a tropical grassland with scattered trees, such as in East Africa?
x: The Serengeti in Tanzania is a famous savanna, home to the great wildebeest migration.

q: The island of Tasmania is part of which country?
x: Tasmania is the only Australian state that is an island. It lies south of the state of Victoria.

q: Which river flows through Rome?
x: Legend says the city's founders, Romulus and Remus, were abandoned as babies on the banks of the Tiber.

q: Which river flows through Baghdad?
x: The Tigris and Euphrates enclose ancient Mesopotamia, whose name means 'land between the rivers'.

q: The River Danube flows into which sea?
x: The Danube ends in a large delta in Romania and Ukraine, one of Europe's best wetlands for birds.

q: Which river flows through Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade?
x: The Danube passes through or along ten countries, more than any other river in the world.

q: Which strait separates Asia from North America?
x: At its narrowest it is about 82 km wide. During the Ice Age a land bridge here let people walk from Asia into the Americas.

q: Istanbul is split between Europe and Asia by which strait?
x: The Bosporus links the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara and is only about 700 m wide at its narrowest.

q: Which canal links the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea?
x: Opened in 1869, the Suez Canal lets ships between Europe and Asia avoid sailing all the way around Africa.

q: Which desert covers much of Botswana?
x: The Kalahari gets more rain than a true desert, so much of it is covered in grass and thorn bushes.

q: The White Nile flows out of which large African lake?
x: The river leaves Lake Victoria at Jinja in Uganda. Lake Victoria is shared by Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania.

q: The Blue Nile begins at Lake Tana in which country?
x: Although the White Nile is longer, the Blue Nile supplies most of the water reaching Egypt, especially in the rainy season.

q: Lake Titicaca lies on the border of Peru and which country?
x: At about 3,800 m above sea level, Titicaca is often called the highest navigable lake in the world.

q: Which river forms much of the border between the United States and Mexico?
x: In Mexico the river is called the Río Bravo del Norte.

q: Which is the longest river in Asia?
x: The Yangtze flows about 6,300 km across China, and the Three Gorges Dam on it is the world's largest power station.

q: Which is the highest mountain in South America?
x: Aconcagua, in Argentina, is about 6,960 m high, the highest mountain anywhere outside Asia.

q: Which is the highest mountain in the United Kingdom?
x: Ben Nevis, near Fort William in Scotland, is about 1,345 m high.

q: Which mountain range stretches across Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia?
x: The Atlas separate the Mediterranean coast from the Sahara. Their highest peak is Toubkal in Morocco.

q: The volcano Krakatoa, whose 1883 eruption was heard thousands of kilometres away, is in which country?
x: The 1883 explosion was heard on Rodrigues Island, near Mauritius, almost 4,800 km away.

q: Which volcano in Washington State erupted violently in May 1980?
x: The eruption blew about 400 m off the top of the mountain.

q: In which country did the 2010 Eyjafjallajökull eruption ground flights across Europe?
x: The ash cloud closed much of European airspace for about six days, the biggest air-travel shutdown since the Second World War.

q: Iceland sits on which plate boundary, where the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart?
x: At Þingvellir in Iceland you can walk in the rift valley between the two plates.

q: The Himalayas were pushed up by the Indian Plate colliding with which plate?
x: The collision is still going on, so the Himalayas are still rising by a few millimetres each year.

q: What name is given to the supercontinent that began breaking apart about 200 million years ago?
x: Pangaea means 'all lands'. It split first into Laurasia in the north and Gondwana in the south. Rodinia and Pannotia were older supercontinents that broke up long before.

q: Which huge valley in East Africa marks where the continent is slowly splitting apart?
x: In millions of years the rift may open up into a new ocean, separating the Horn of Africa from the rest of the continent.

q: What is the point on the Earth's surface directly above the start of an earthquake called?
x: The focus (or hypocentre) is the point underground where the rock first breaks; the epicentre is right above it.

q: The deepest known point in the oceans, Challenger Deep, is in which trench?
x: Challenger Deep, in the western Pacific, is nearly 11 km deep, deeper than Everest is tall.

q: Which sea lies between Saudi Arabia and north-east Africa?
x: The Red Sea is one of the saltiest seas connected to the ocean, because it is very hot and few rivers flow into it.

q: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania all have a coast on which sea?
x: The Baltic is brackish, much less salty than the open ocean, because so many rivers flow into it.

q: Which sea, dotted with islands, lies between mainland Greece and Turkey?
x: The Aegean contains thousands of islands, including the Cyclades and the Dodecanese.

q: Along with Bolivia, which South American country is landlocked?
x: Paraguay still has a navy, which patrols its rivers, the Paraguay and the Paraná.

q: Which of these South-East Asian countries is landlocked?
x: Laos is the only landlocked country in South-East Asia. The Mekong River forms much of its border with Thailand.

q: Which of these European countries is landlocked?
x: Hungary's largest lake, Lake Balaton, is sometimes called the 'Hungarian sea'.

q: Since Eritrea became independent in 1993, which African country has had no coastline?
x: Ethiopia mainly uses the port of Djibouti for its trade.

q: Besides Vatican City, which country is completely surrounded by Italy?
x: San Marino claims to be the world's oldest surviving republic, traditionally founded in AD 301.

q: Which small country lies in the Pyrenees between France and Spain?
x: Andorra has two co-princes as joint heads of state: the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell in Spain.

q: Haiti shares the island of Hispaniola with which country?
x: Hispaniola is the second-largest island in the Caribbean, after Cuba.

q: The Galápagos Islands belong to which country?
x: The islands lie about 1,000 km off the coast. Their unique wildlife helped inspire Charles Darwin's ideas on evolution.

q: The Faroe Islands are a self-governing part of which kingdom?
x: The Faroes lie roughly halfway between Norway and Iceland, north-west of Scotland, and are home to about 55,000 people (as of 2024).

q: Honshu is the main island of which country?
x: Japan has four main islands: Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu and Shikoku. Tokyo, Osaka and Kyoto are all on Honshu.

q: The Drake Passage separates the southern tip of South America from which continent?
x: The Drake Passage is famous for some of the roughest seas in the world. It is named after the explorer Sir Francis Drake.

q: The Cape of Good Hope is in which country?
x: Despite a popular belief, it is not Africa's southernmost point: that is Cape Agulhas, about 150 km to the south-east.

q: Which line of latitude lies at about 23.4° south of the Equator?
x: It marks the furthest south the Sun can be directly overhead. It passes through Australia, southern Africa and Brazil.

q: North of which line can you see the midnight sun at the June solstice?
x: North of the Arctic Circle the Sun stays up for 24 hours on at least one day a year, and does not rise on at least one day in winter.

q: What is the seasonal wind that brings heavy summer rain to South Asia called?
x: India gets most of its yearly rain during the summer monsoon, usually from June to September.

x: Below the surface of the tundra is permafrost, ground that stays frozen all year round.

x: All of China runs on Beijing Time (UTC+8), so in the far west the Sun can rise as late as 10 am in winter.

q: The International Date Line runs mostly through which ocean?
x: It zigzags around island groups so that no country is split between two different calendar days.

q: Which major US city lies on the shore of Lake Michigan?
x: Lake Michigan is the only one of the five Great Lakes that lies entirely inside the United States.

q: Which Russian city is built on the delta of the River Neva?

q: Which river flows through the German cities of Cologne and Düsseldorf?
x: The Rhine rises in the Swiss Alps and reaches the North Sea in the Netherlands.

q: Which river connects the Great Lakes to the Atlantic Ocean?
x: Montreal and Quebec City both stand on the St Lawrence, and the St Lawrence Seaway lets ships sail from the ocean to the Great Lakes.

x: Iguazu is a system of around 275 separate waterfalls spread along nearly 3 km of the Iguazu River.

q: Lake Geneva is shared by Switzerland and which country?
x: The River Rhône flows into Lake Geneva at one end and out of it again at Geneva.

q: Death Valley, the lowest point in North America, is in which US state?

q: The Namib, often called the world's oldest desert, is mainly in which country?
x: The Namib runs along the Atlantic coast, and its towering red sand dunes are among the highest in the world.

q: What is a fertile spot in a desert, where water reaches the surface, called?
x: Oases have been vital stopping points for desert travellers and their camels for thousands of years.

q: What is a ring-shaped coral reef or island surrounding a lagoon called?
x: Atolls usually form when a coral reef grows around a volcanic island that then slowly sinks beneath the sea.

q: The summit of Mount Everest lies on the border between Nepal and which country?
x: Climbers can approach Everest from the south side in Nepal or the north side in Tibet, China.

q: Which mountain range stretches between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea?
x: Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan are often called the countries of the Caucasus.

q: Which warm ocean current helps give the British Isles mild winters?
x: The Gulf Stream carries warm water from the Gulf of Mexico across the Atlantic, where its extension is called the North Atlantic Drift.

q: In the north-west Pacific Ocean, what are hurricanes called?
x: Hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are all the same kind of storm; only the name changes depending on the ocean.

q: What is the main cause of the Earth's seasons?
x: Earth is tilted by about 23.4°. In fact, Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during the northern winter.

x: The Severn is about 354 km long, rising in Wales and reaching the sea in the Bristol Channel. The Thames is a close second.

q: Tenerife and Gran Canaria are part of which island group?

q: Mongolia shares land borders with only two countries. Which?
x: Kazakhstan comes very close to Mongolia, but the two are separated by a narrow strip of Russian and Chinese land.

q: Mount Etna, one of Europe's most active volcanoes, is on which island?
x: Etna erupts very often, yet people farm its slopes because volcanic soil is so fertile.

x: Five countries border the Caspian: Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Azerbaijan, whose capital Baku is on its shore.

x: Rivers feeding the Aral were diverted to water cotton fields, and it lost most of its water, leaving ships stranded in desert.

q: Which island is divided between Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei?
x: Borneo is the third-largest island in the world, and Brunei is the only country that lies entirely on it.

q: Which Caribbean island is split between France and the Netherlands?

q: Which strait separates Tasmania from mainland Australia?

q: Germany's Kiel Canal links the North Sea to which sea?
x: The canal, opened in 1895, saves ships a journey of several hundred kilometres around the tip of Denmark.

x: Haiti and the Dominican Republic together have over 20 million people, about twice as many as Cuba.

q: Which is the largest island in the United States?
x: The island of Hawaii covers about 10,400 km², and it is still growing as its volcanoes add new land.

q: Which is the largest of the Canary Islands?
x: Tenerife covers about 2,000 km² and has Spain's highest mountain, Mount Teide.

q: Which is the largest island in Scotland?
x: Lewis and Harris is one island, despite its name, and the third-largest in the British Isles after Great Britain and Ireland.

q: Not counting Great Britain itself, which is the largest island in England?
x: The Isle of Wight covers about 380 km² and has around 140,000 people.

q: Which is the largest island in South America?
a: Isla Grande de Tierra del Fuego
x: The main island of Tierra del Fuego, at the continent's southern tip, is shared by Chile and Argentina.

q: Which is the largest island in a freshwater lake?
x: Manitoulin, in Lake Huron, covers about 2,800 km² and has more than 100 lakes of its own.

q: Which is the largest lake in the European Union by area?
x: Vänern in Sweden covers about 5,650 km². Bigger lakes in Europe, like Ladoga, are in Russia.

q: Which is the largest lake in Great Britain by surface area?
x: Loch Lomond covers about 71 km². Lough Neagh, the UK's largest lake, is in Northern Ireland, not Great Britain.

q: Which is the largest lake that lies entirely within Canada?
x: Great Bear Lake in the Northwest Territories covers about 31,000 km² and is crossed by the Arctic Circle.

q: Which is the largest lake in Australia?
x: This salt lake in South Australia is usually dry, and fills completely only rarely, after exceptional rains.

q: Which is the world's largest reservoir by surface area?
x: Lake Volta in Ghana formed behind the Akosombo Dam in the 1960s and covers about 8,500 km². Lake Kariba holds more water.

q: Which is the third-largest country in South America by area?
x: Peru covers about 1.29 million km², ahead of Colombia at about 1.14 million km².

q: Which is the seventh-largest country in the world by area?
x: Australia is sixth; India covers about 3.3 million km², followed by Argentina and Kazakhstan.

q: Which is the largest country in mainland Southeast Asia by area?
x: Myanmar covers about 677,000 km², ahead of Thailand at about 513,000 km².

q: Which is the fifth-largest continent by area?
x: Antarctica covers about 14 million km², bigger than Europe or Australia, and is almost all ice.

q: Greenland and Africa look similar in size on many world maps. Roughly how many times bigger is Africa?
x: The common Mercator map stretches land near the poles. Greenland is about 2.2 million km²; Africa about 30 million km².

q: Which is the smallest country in Asia by area?
x: The Maldives' 1,000-plus coral islands add up to only about 300 km² of land.

q: Which is the smallest country in Africa by area?
x: The Seychelles' islands add up to about 460 km², and its 2022 census counted about 120,000 people.

q: Which is the smallest country in the Americas by area?
x: The two islands cover about 260 km² and have under 50,000 people.

q: Which is the world's smallest island country by area?
x: Nauru in the Pacific covers about 21 km², making it the third-smallest country in the world after Vatican City and Monaco.

q: About how many people live in Vatican City (as of 2024)?
x: Only a few hundred people live there, mostly clergy and Swiss Guards, making it the least populous country too.

q: Which landlocked country has the most people (as of 2024)?
x: Ethiopia has about 130 million people. It lost its coastline when Eritrea became independent in 1993.

q: Among countries with over 100 million people, which is the most densely populated?
x: Bangladesh has over 1,000 people per km², more than twice India's density.

q: Which of these countries has the most people (as of 2024)?
x: Bangladesh has about 173 million people in about 148,000 km², a little less than England and Wales combined. It is the eighth most populous country.

q: Which country in Central Asia has the most people (as of 2024)?
x: Uzbekistan has about 36 million people; Kazakhstan is far bigger by area but has about 20 million.

q: Which country in the European Union is the least densely populated?
x: Finland has under 20 people per km², and most of them live in the south.

q: Which is the largest city in Bolivia by population?
x: Santa Cruz in the eastern lowlands has grown fast thanks to farming and gas, overtaking La Paz.

q: Which is the largest city in Kazakhstan by population?
x: Almaty was the capital until 1997, when the government moved north to Astana.

q: Which is the largest city in Côte d'Ivoire by population?
x: Abidjan has more than 5 million people. Yamoussoukro became the official capital in 1983.

q: Within city limits, which is Poland's second-largest city by population?
x: Kraków has about 800,000 people and was Poland's royal capital for centuries.

q: Within city limits, which is Argentina's second-largest city by population?
x: Córdoba has about 1.5 million people. Greater Buenos Aires is many times bigger.

q: Which is the largest Indian state by area?
x: Rajasthan covers about 342,000 km², much of it the Thar Desert. It took the top spot when Madhya Pradesh was split in 2000.

q: Which is the largest Brazilian state by area?
x: Amazonas covers about 1.6 million km², bigger than France, Spain and Germany combined, but has only about 4 million people.

q: Which is the most populous German state?
x: North Rhine-Westphalia, home to Cologne and Düsseldorf, has about 18 million people.

q: Which is the smallest German state by area?
x: Bremen is a city-state made up of two cities, Bremen and Bremerhaven, covering about 420 km².

q: Which is the largest of Russia's federal subjects by area?
x: Sakha in Siberia covers about 3 million km², nearly the size of India, but has only about a million people.

q: Which is the largest Mexican state by area?
x: Chihuahua, bordering Texas and New Mexico, covers about 247,000 km².

q: Which is the largest of Spain's autonomous communities by area?
x: Castile and León covers about 94,000 km², slightly more than Andalusia.

q: Which is the largest region of mainland France by area?
x: Nouvelle-Aquitaine in the south-west, which includes Bordeaux, covers about 84,000 km².

q: Which Chinese province has the most people?
x: Guangdong, around Guangzhou and Shenzhen, has over 125 million people.

q: Which is the largest province of Pakistan by area?
x: Balochistan covers about 44% of Pakistan's land but has the fewest people of its four provinces.

q: Which is the largest county in Ireland by area?
x: County Cork covers about 7,500 km² on the south coast.

q: Which is the largest principal area (county) in Wales by area?
x: Powys covers about a quarter of Wales but has only around 130,000 people.

q: Which is the largest ceremonial county in England by area?
x: North Yorkshire covers more than 8,000 km², including the Yorkshire Dales and North York Moors.

q: Which country has the lowest fertility rate in the world (as of 2024)?
x: South Korea's rate fell to about 0.7 children per woman in 2023, far below the replacement level of about 2.1.

q: Which country has the world's youngest population, with the lowest median age?
x: Half of Niger's people are younger than about 15, according to UN estimates.

q: According to the UN's 2024 projections, roughly when will the world's population peak?
x: The UN expects a peak of about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s, followed by a slow decline.

q: About how many people did the first US census count, in 1790?
x: The 1790 census counted about 3.9 million people. The US now has more than 80 times as many.

q: Roughly what share of Egypt's people live in the Nile Valley and Delta?
x: Only about 5% of Egypt's land is lived on; the rest is mostly desert.

q: About three-quarters of Russia's area is in Asia. Roughly what share of its people live there?
x: Most Russians live west of the Ural Mountains, in the European part of the country.

q: In which city is the clock tower known as Big Ben?
x: Big Ben is strictly the name of the great bell inside. The tower itself was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012.

q: In which Italian city is the famous Leaning Tower?
x: Building began in 1173 and the tower started to tilt during construction because the ground on one side is soft.

q: Which Australian city's harbour is home to an opera house with sail-shaped roofs?
x: The Sydney Opera House opened in 1973 and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007.

q: In which city is the Parthenon?
x: The temple was built on the Acropolis in the 5th century BC and was dedicated to the goddess Athena.

q: In which city are the Kremlin and Red Square?
x: St Basil's Cathedral, with its colourful onion domes, was built on Red Square in the 1550s on the orders of Ivan the Terrible.

q: Which famous statue near the Egyptian pyramids has a lion's body and a human head?
x: Carved from a single ridge of limestone, it is one of the largest and oldest monumental statues in the world.

q: How many US presidents' faces are carved into Mount Rushmore?
x: Washington, Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Lincoln were carved into the South Dakota mountain between 1927 and 1941.

q: In which city is the Forbidden City?
x: It was the imperial palace of the Ming and Qing emperors from 1420 until the last emperor abdicated in 1912.

q: In which country is Uluru, the giant red sandstone rock also called Ayers Rock?
x: Uluru stands in the Northern Territory and is sacred to the Anangu, the Aboriginal people of the area.

q: Which city's skyline is home to the Empire State Building?
x: It opened in 1931 after little more than a year of building, and stayed the world's tallest building until 1970.

q: In which city is the CN Tower?
x: Finished in 1976 at about 553 m, it was the world's tallest freestanding structure for over 30 years.

q: Which London landmark is home to the Crown Jewels?
x: William the Conqueror founded the Tower after 1066. The jewels are kept in its Jewel House.

q: Buckingham Palace is the official London residence of whom?
x: It became the monarch's main London residence when Queen Victoria moved in in 1837.

q: Which Paris museum has a large glass pyramid at its entrance?
x: The pyramid was designed by the architect I. M. Pei and completed in 1989.

q: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
x: He painted the ceiling between 1508 and 1512, and returned decades later to paint The Last Judgement on the altar wall.

q: In which city is the Trevi Fountain?
x: Visitors throw coins over their shoulder into it. The coins are collected and given to charity.

q: In which city is St Mark's Square?
x: The square is the city's main public space, overlooked by St Mark's Basilica and the Doge's Palace.

q: The Pyramids of Giza stand on the edge of which city?
x: Giza is now part of Greater Cairo, and the city's suburbs reach almost to the foot of the pyramids.

q: Which city is overlooked by the flat-topped Table Mountain?
x: A cable car has carried visitors to the top since 1929.

q: The former prison of Alcatraz is on an island in which bay?
x: It was a US federal prison from 1934 to 1963 and is now a museum.

q: In which city are the Petronas Twin Towers?
x: They were the tallest buildings in the world from 1998 until Taipei 101 overtook them in 2004.

q: In which city is the Marina Bay Sands hotel, with a park on its roof?
x: Its three towers are joined at the top by the SkyPark. It opened in 2010.

q: The Hobbiton movie set can be visited in which country?
x: It was built on a farm near Matamata for The Lord of the Rings and rebuilt to last for The Hobbit films.

q: Hadrian's Wall marked the northern frontier of which empire?
x: Building began in AD 122 under Emperor Hadrian. The wall ran about 117 km across northern England.

q: In which city can you visit the Anne Frank House?
x: Anne Frank and her family hid in the secret annexe behind the building from 1942 to 1944.

q: Which United Nations agency keeps the list of World Heritage Sites?
x: The first sites were added to the list in 1978.

q: In which city is the Ponte Vecchio, a medieval bridge lined with shops?
x: It was the only bridge in Florence not destroyed by German forces as they retreated in 1944.

q: Cappadocia, famous for its 'fairy chimney' rock towers and hot-air balloons, is in which country?
x: People carved homes, churches and even whole underground cities into its soft volcanic rock.

q: In which country is Ha Long Bay, with its thousands of limestone islands?
x: The bay became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994.

q: In which city is the Hermitage Museum?
x: Catherine the Great founded the collection in 1764. Part of the museum is in the Winter Palace of the tsars.

q: Michelangelo's statue of David is displayed in which city?
x: The original stands in the Accademia gallery. A copy took its old place outside the Palazzo Vecchio.

q: In which Spanish city is the Prado, one of Europe's great art museums?
x: It opened in 1819 and holds major works by Velázquez, Goya and El Greco.

q: Which Italian city is famous for its canals and gondolas?
x: The city is built on more than 100 small islands in a lagoon, linked by about 400 bridges.

q: In which city is the Atomium, a giant model of an iron crystal?
x: It was built for the 1958 World's Fair and shows an iron crystal magnified 165 billion times.

q: The Terracotta Army was found near which Chinese city?
x: The clay soldiers were buried with China's first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, and were discovered by farmers digging a well in 1974.

q: The Grand Canyon is in which US state?
x: It was carved by the Colorado River and is more than 1.6 km deep in places.

q: The Space Needle tower was built for a World's Fair in which city?
x: It was built for the 1962 World's Fair and has a revolving glass floor near the top.

q: In which city is the Little Mermaid statue?
x: The small bronze statue was unveiled in 1913 and is based on the fairy tale by Hans Christian Andersen.

q: In which city is the Manneken Pis statue?
x: The little bronze boy on the street corner is a copy. The older original is kept in the city's museum.

q: Which ruler commissioned the Arc de Triomphe in Paris?
x: He ordered it in 1806 after his victory at Austerlitz, but it was not finished until 1836. It stands at the top of the Champs-Élysées.

q: The Palace of Versailles was turned into a vast royal palace by which French king?
x: The Sun King moved his court there in 1682. The treaty ending the First World War was signed in its Hall of Mirrors in 1919.

q: In which year did a fire destroy the roof and spire of Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris?
x: The fire broke out in April 2019. The restored cathedral reopened in December 2024.

q: Venice's Rialto Bridge crosses which waterway?
x: The stone bridge was completed in 1591, and for centuries it was the only way to cross the Grand Canal on foot.

q: Who designed the great dome of Florence Cathedral?
x: The dome was completed in 1436 and is still the largest brick dome ever built.

q: In which Egyptian city's area is the Valley of the Kings?
x: Howard Carter found the tomb of Tutankhamun there in 1922.

q: Which famous prisoner spent 18 years on Robben Island?
x: The island off Cape Town was a prison for political prisoners and is now a museum and UNESCO World Heritage Site.

q: The Nazca Lines, giant drawings in the desert best seen from the air, are in which country?
x: They were made about 2,000 years ago by scraping away the dark surface stones to reveal lighter ground beneath.

q: In which year did the Panama Canal open?
x: The United States began building it in 1904. The Suez Canal had opened in 1869.

q: What did the Hollywood sign in Los Angeles originally spell out?
x: It was put up in 1923 to advertise a housing estate. The last four letters were removed in 1949.

q: The Brooklyn Bridge links Brooklyn with which other part of New York City?
x: It crosses the East River. Its granite towers were among the tallest structures in the city when it opened in 1883.

q: The Gateway Arch, the world's tallest arch, is in which US city?
x: Finished in 1965, the stainless-steel arch is 192 m tall and celebrates the city's role as the 'gateway to the West'.

q: What is the street address of the White House?
x: John Adams was the first president to live there, moving in in 1800.

q: Which is generally considered the world's first national park?
x: It was created in 1872 and is home to the Old Faithful geyser. Most of the park is in Wyoming.

q: In which city is the Burj Al Arab, a sail-shaped hotel on its own artificial island?
x: The hotel opened in 1999 and stands on an island linked to the shore by a curving bridge.

q: In which city is the Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque?
x: Completed in 2007, it is one of the largest mosques in the world and has one of the largest hand-knotted carpets.

q: The Golden Temple in Amritsar is the most important shrine of which religion?
x: Its upper floors are covered in gold, and its community kitchen serves free meals to tens of thousands of people a day.

q: In which city is India Gate, a war memorial designed by Edwin Lutyens?
x: Completed in 1931, it bears the names of Indian soldiers who died in the First World War.

q: The Gateway of India arch overlooks the sea in which city?
x: It was built to mark the visit of King George V in 1911 and finished in 1924.

q: Which Japanese shrine is famous for its tunnels of thousands of orange torii gates?
x: The Kyoto shrine is dedicated to Inari, the god of rice. Each gate is donated by a person or business.

q: In which city is Kinkaku-ji, the Golden Pavilion?
x: Its top floors are covered in gold leaf. The building seen today was rebuilt in 1955 after a monk burned it down in 1950.

q: The Genbaku Dome, a ruined building kept as a peace memorial, is in which Japanese city?
x: It was one of the few buildings left standing near the centre of the 1945 atomic blast, and became a World Heritage Site in 1996.

q: In which city is the Oriental Pearl Tower?
x: The TV tower, with its pink spheres, opened in 1994 on the Pudong side of the Huangpu River.

q: In which city are the Grand Palace and the temple of Wat Arun?
x: The Grand Palace was the royal residence from 1782 and is still used for state ceremonies. It contains the Temple of the Emerald Buddha.

q: What is the Sydney Harbour Bridge's well-known nickname?
x: The steel arch bridge opened in 1932. Visitors can climb over the top of the arch.

q: The architect of the Sydney Opera House, Jørn Utzon, came from which country?
x: Utzon won the design competition in 1957 but left the project in 1966, years before it opened.

q: The Great Barrier Reef lies off the coast of which Australian state?
x: It is the world's largest coral reef system and stretches more than 2,300 km.

q: Milford Sound, a famous fiord visited by cruise boats, is in which country?
x: It is in Fiordland National Park on the South Island.

q: The Giant's Causeway, made of about 40,000 basalt columns, is in which part of the UK?
x: The columns formed as lava cooled around 50 to 60 million years ago. Legend says the giant Finn McCool built it.

q: Which is often described as the oldest and largest occupied castle in the world?
x: William the Conqueror founded it in the 11th century, and it is still a working royal residence.

q: Who designed St Paul's Cathedral in London?
x: It replaced the old cathedral lost in the Great Fire of 1666 and was finished in the early 1700s.

q: Which London church has hosted every English and British coronation since 1066?
x: William the Conqueror was crowned there on Christmas Day 1066, and Charles III in 2023.

q: The Angel of the North sculpture stands beside which town?
x: Antony Gormley's steel angel was put up in 1998. Its wings are 54 m across, almost as wide as a jumbo jet's.

q: According to legend, what does kissing the Blarney Stone give you?
x: The stone is set in the wall of Blarney Castle near Cork, and you have to lean backwards over a drop to kiss it.

q: In which country are the Cliffs of Moher?
x: The cliffs in County Clare rise over 200 m above the Atlantic at their highest point.

q: Kinderdijk, a UNESCO site with 19 windmills from the 1700s, is in which country?
x: The windmills were built around 1740 to pump water out of the low-lying land.

q: Which German city's Gothic cathedral took more than 600 years to finish?
x: Work began in 1248 and ended in 1880. For a few years after that it was the tallest building in the world.

q: In which city is the Charles Bridge?
x: Building began in 1357 under King Charles IV, and the bridge is lined with 30 statues.

q: Who designed the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao?
x: The curving, titanium-covered museum opened in 1997 and helped transform the city.

q: Which architect designed Park Güell in Barcelona?
x: The park was first planned as a housing estate for wealthy families and opened as a public park in 1926.

q: In which city is the Belém Tower?
x: Built in the early 16th century to guard the mouth of the River Tagus, it is a symbol of Portugal's Age of Discovery.

q: In which city can you see Leonardo da Vinci's mural The Last Supper?
x: It is painted on the wall of the dining hall of the convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie.

q: Meteora, where monasteries sit on top of tall rock pillars, is in which country?
x: Monks began building there in the 14th century. Supplies were once hauled up in nets.

q: The ancient Oracle of Delphi spoke at a temple to which god?
x: The oracle was a priestess called the Pythia, and people travelled from across the Greek world to consult her.

q: On which island is the Minoan palace of Knossos?
x: It is linked to the legend of King Minos and the labyrinth of the Minotaur.

q: The ruins of Ephesus, with its Library of Celsus, are in which country?
x: Ephesus was a major Greek and then Roman city on the Aegean coast.

q: Plitvice Lakes National Park, with its chain of turquoise lakes and waterfalls, is in which country?
x: It was one of the first natural sites added to the UNESCO World Heritage list, in 1979.

q: Mont-Saint-Michel, a tidal island topped by an abbey, lies off the coast of which French region?
x: At high tide the sea surrounds the island, which is now reached by a raised bridge.

q: Paris's Musée d'Orsay is housed in a former what?
x: The Gare d'Orsay was built for the 1900 World's Fair. The museum opened in 1986.

q: In which museum is the Rosetta Stone displayed?
x: It has been on display in London since 1802. Its three scripts helped scholars decode Egyptian hieroglyphs.

q: Who sculpted the Statue of Liberty?
x: Bartholdi designed the statue, while Eiffel's company built the iron frame inside it.

q: Which dam on the Colorado River created Lake Mead?
x: Completed in 1936, it straddles the border between Nevada and Arizona.

q: The Hassan II Mosque, whose minaret is among the tallest in the world, is in which city?
x: It was completed in 1993 and is built partly over the Atlantic Ocean.

q: Jemaa el-Fnaa, a square packed with storytellers, musicians and food stalls, is in which city?
x: It is the heart of the city's old medina and comes alive in the evening.

q: The ruins of ancient Carthage lie on the edge of which modern city?
x: Carthage was a great Phoenician city and Rome's rival until the Romans destroyed it in 146 BC.

q: Victoria Falls is known locally as Mosi-oa-Tunya. What does that mean?
x: The falls lie between Zambia and Zimbabwe. David Livingstone named them after Queen Victoria in 1855.

q: In which country is the Salar de Uyuni, the world's largest salt flat?
x: It covers more than 10,000 km², and after rain it turns into a giant mirror.

q: The Chocolate Hills, which turn brown in the dry season, are in which country?
x: There are over a thousand of these grassy cone-shaped hills on the island of Bohol.

q: The Øresund Bridge links Copenhagen with which Swedish city?
x: Opened in 2000, the route switches from bridge to tunnel at an artificial island called Peberholm.

q: Himeji Castle, one of the best-preserved feudal castles of its kind, is in which country?
x: Its brilliant white walls earned it the nickname 'White Heron Castle'.

q: Edinburgh Castle stands on the plug of what?
x: Castle Rock formed from volcanic rock around 350 million years ago, and ice later scraped away the softer land around it.

q: Which pharaoh built the great temples at Abu Simbel?
x: In the 1960s the temples were cut into blocks and moved uphill to save them from the lake behind the Aswan High Dam.

q: The Great Mosque of Djenné, the world's largest mud-brick building, is in which country?
x: The present building dates from 1907, and the townspeople replaster it with fresh mud every year.

q: The rock-hewn churches of Lalibela are in which country?
x: The churches were carved down into solid rock, traditionally in the time of King Lalibela around the 12th to 13th century.

q: The country Zimbabwe is named after which ancient site?
x: Its huge stone walls were built without mortar between the 11th and 15th centuries.

q: The Pyramid of the Sun stands in which ancient city?
x: The city lies north-east of modern Mexico City. Its name was given to it centuries later by the Aztecs.

q: The ruined Maya city of Tikal is in which country?
x: Its temple-pyramids rise above the rainforest canopy, and it was one of the most powerful Maya cities.

q: As of 2026, the world's tallest statue, the Statue of Unity, is in which country?
x: Opened in 2018, the 182 m statue depicts the independence leader Vallabhbhai Patel.

q: In which city is the gilded Shwedagon Pagoda?
x: The pagoda is covered in gold and its top is studded with thousands of diamonds and other gems.

q: Sigiriya, a 5th-century palace on top of a huge rock, is in which country?
x: King Kashyapa built his palace on the summit, reached through a gateway shaped like a giant lion.

q: In which Indian city is the Hawa Mahal, the 'Palace of Winds'?
x: Built in 1799, its many small windows let royal women watch street life without being seen.

q: As of 2026, the world's tallest broadcasting tower rises over which city?
x: The Tokyo Skytree, a broadcasting tower, is 634 m tall and opened in 2012.

q: In which country were the giant Buddhas of Bamiyan destroyed in 2001?
x: The two statues, carved into a cliff about 1,500 years ago, were blown up by the Taliban.

q: The Registan, a square framed by three grand madrasas, is in which city?
x: Samarkand was a great stop on the Silk Road and is now in Uzbekistan.

q: Gyeongbokgung, the main royal palace of the Joseon dynasty, is in which city?
x: It was first built in 1395. Much of it was destroyed in the 20th century and has since been restored.

q: Who designed The Shard in London?
x: Finished in 2012, the 310 m tower is the tallest building in the UK as of 2026.

q: Who designed the glass dome on top of Berlin's Reichstag building?
x: It opened in 1999. Visitors walk up a spiral ramp above the debating chamber of the German parliament.

q: The Mezquita, a mosque-cathedral full of red-and-white arches, is in which city?
x: Building began in 785, and a cathedral was built in the middle of it in the 16th century.

q: Istanbul's Blue Mosque is officially named after which Ottoman sultan?
x: The Sultan Ahmed Mosque was completed in 1616. Its nickname comes from the blue tiles inside.

q: What is displayed in Stockholm's Vasa Museum?
x: The Vasa sank on its maiden voyage in 1628, was raised in 1961, and is about 98% original.

q: The Pont du Gard in southern France was built by the Romans as part of what?
x: Built in the 1st century AD, the three-tiered bridge is almost 50 m high and carried water to the city of Nîmes.

q: Eva Perón is buried in which Buenos Aires cemetery?
x: Recoleta Cemetery is a maze of grand family tombs. She lies in the Duarte family vault.

q: Elmina Castle, built by the Portuguese in 1482, is in which modern country?
x: It is one of the oldest European-built buildings south of the Sahara and later became a centre of the Atlantic slave trade.

q: Angkor Wat was originally built as a temple to which Hindu god?
x: King Suryavarman II built it in the 12th century. It later became a Buddhist temple.

q: The ancient Lighthouse of Alexandria stood on which island?
x: The island's name became the word for lighthouse in several languages, such as 'phare' in French.

q: The word 'mausoleum' comes from the tomb of Mausolus in which ancient city?
x: The tomb was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. The site is in modern Bodrum, Turkey.

q: Which sculptor made the Statue of Zeus at Olympia, one of the Seven Wonders?
x: The seated figure was made of ivory and gold. Phidias also oversaw the sculptures of the Parthenon.

q: As of 2026, the world's longest suspension bridge span is the 1915 Çanakkale Bridge. What does it cross?
x: Opened in 2022, its main span is 2,023 m, a number chosen for the republic's centenary in 2023.

q: Which architect designed Fallingwater, a house built over a waterfall in Pennsylvania?
x: Designed in 1935 for the Kaufmann family, it is now a museum.

q: Which architect designed the cathedral and main government buildings of Brasília?
x: Lúcio Costa drew the plan of the city, which is shaped a little like an aeroplane or bird.

q: Le Corbusier planned which Indian city?
x: Built in the 1950s, it is the capital of two states, Punjab and Haryana.

q: Which is the closest star to Earth?
x: The next nearest star, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.

q: What is the name of the galaxy that contains our Solar System?
x: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy thought to hold somewhere between 100 and 400 billion stars.

q: Which former planet was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006?
x: The International Astronomical Union's new definition of a planet left the Solar System with eight planets.

q: Which is the hottest planet in the Solar System?
x: Although Mercury is closer to the Sun, Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, keeping its surface at around 460 °C.

q: Who was the first human to travel into space, in 1961?
x: Gagarin made one orbit of Earth aboard Vostok 1 on 12 April 1961.

q: Roughly how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
x: Light covers the 150 million km from the Sun in about 8 minutes 20 seconds, so we see the Sun as it was that long ago.

q: What is the boundary around a black hole, beyond which nothing can escape, called?
x: Not even light can get back out once it crosses the event horizon, which is why black holes look black.

q: Which is the largest moon in the Solar System?
x: Jupiter's moon Ganymede is even bigger than the planet Mercury, though it has less mass.

q: Which astronomer worked out three laws of planetary motion, including that orbits are ellipses?
x: Kepler's first law says each planet moves in an ellipse with the Sun at one focus, not in a perfect circle.

q: Who described a Sun-centred Solar System in a book published in 1543, the year he died?
x: His book De revolutionibus orbium coelestium put the Sun, not Earth, at the centre.

q: What is the SI unit of electric charge?
x: One coulomb is the charge carried by a current of one ampere flowing for one second.

q: What is the chemical symbol for iron?
x: Fe comes from ferrum, the Latin word for iron, which also gives us the word 'ferrous'.

q: What is the chemical formula for table salt?
x: Table salt is sodium chloride: one sodium atom for every chlorine atom.

q: Which metal is liquid at room temperature and was once common in thermometers?
x: Mercury freezes at about -39 °C, so it stays liquid in all ordinary conditions.

q: Diamond and graphite are both made of which element?
x: The difference is how the atoms are arranged: graphite is soft enough to be the 'lead' in pencils.

q: Which acid does the human stomach produce to help digest food?
x: A layer of mucus stops the stomach from digesting its own lining.

q: What is the chemical symbol for tungsten?
x: W comes from wolfram, its German name. Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal.

q: Which is the most abundant element in Earth's crust by mass?

q: How many chambers does the human heart have?

q: What is the largest organ of the human body?
x: An adult's skin weighs several kilograms and covers an area of about 2 square metres.

q: Which organs filter the blood to make urine?

q: What process do plants use to turn sunlight, water and carbon dioxide into food?

q: Which part of a cell is often called its powerhouse?

q: Which blood type can be given to almost anyone in an emergency?

q: Which organ produces insulin?
x: Insulin was first used to treat a person with diabetes in Toronto in 1922.

q: Which coloured part of the eye controls the size of the pupil?
x: The pupil is just the opening; the muscles of the iris widen or shrink it to let in more or less light.

q: How many chromosomes do human body cells usually contain?
x: They come in 23 pairs: one of each pair from the mother and one from the father.

q: What is the smallest bone in the human body?
x: The stapes, or stirrup, sits in the middle ear and is only about 3 mm long.

q: Which part of the brain mainly controls balance and coordination?

q: How many legs does a spider have?

q: What is a baby kangaroo called?

q: What do giant pandas mostly eat?

q: Which egg-laying mammal from Australia has a bill like a duck's?
